notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on John 8:1–30. Some limits first. My search budget ran out, and two long pages (Enduring Word and Precept Austin) were cut off partway through, so verses 12–30 are thinner than verses 1–11. I found no pages where Protestant traditions actually disagree with each other over this chapter, and nothing on the "hyper-grace" reading of verse 11. Those parts are left out, as you asked.

---

## Before verse 1: is 7:53–8:11 original to John?

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The manuscripts make it seem unlikely that this portion was part of the original text of John's gospel, or at least in this place. Most of the earliest Greek copies leave it out, many later ones mark it with asterisks, and some place it after Luke 21:38 or elsewhere in John. Even so, Guzik thinks this actually happened, and that John really wrote this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-8/
- **Ligonier (Reformed):** Most scholars don't think John wrote it, but it is an old story that several early church fathers mention, and the church has long held that it records an authentic episode from the life of Christ. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/woman-caught-in-adultery
- **Precept Austin, quoting several teachers:** MacArthur concludes the passage most likely wasn't in John's original text, but that it records a real event and teaches nothing that contradicts the rest of Scripture. Lenski calls the section spurious but accurate, and so gives no exposition of it at all. That is a real difference in how teachers handle the passage: preach it, or set it aside. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-8-commentary
- **The Gospel Coalition (Themelios article):** Few scholars follow Maurice Robinson's defence that the passage is original, and No extant manuscript before the fifth century contains the reading. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/text-criticism-and-the-pulpit-should-one-preach-about-the-woman-caught-in-adultery/
- **GotQuestions:** Gives the case for keeping it (most Greek manuscripts have it, and it may have been dropped early to avoid misunderstanding), but concludes there is serious doubt as to whether it should be included in the Bible. https://www.gotquestions.org/John-7-53-8-11.html
- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey):** most biblical scholars regard this passage as a later addition to the text of the New Testament, probably added after John's Gospel was already circulating without it. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-woman-caught-in-adultery/
- **Catholic (Catholic.com):** Discusses the doubts, noting the story is not found in any surviving manuscripts before Codex Bezae, which dates to the A.D. 400s. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-adulteress-and-the-gospel

---

## Verses 1–11

**v. 1:**
- Ellicott: the chapter break spoils the sense here, and the Mount of Olives isn't mentioned anywhere else in John. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm
- Leon Morris (via Precept Austin): the other Gospels say Jesus taught in Jerusalem by day and slept outside the city, and Luke says He stayed on the Mount of Olives. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-8-commentary
- Augustine (Catholic, via New Advent): plays on the name. Olivet is the "mount of chrism" (anointing oil), a fitting place for the Christ ("Anointed One") to teach. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701033.htm

**v. 2:**
- Guzik: although the authorities wanted to silence Him, Jesus still taught large crowds openly in the temple, the most public place in Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-8/
- Augustine: Jesus wasn't arrested then because He did not yet choose to suffer. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701033.htm

**v. 3:**
- Ligonier: the law punished both man and woman (Lev. 20:10). Charging only the woman shows the leaders didn't really care about the law. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/woman-caught-in-adultery
- Guzik: they brought her in public to shame both her and Jesus. He suggests the missing man may even have been one of the accusers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-8/

**v. 4:**
- Guzik, citing Morris: the legal standard of proof for adultery was so strict it could rarely be met, which points to a set-up. Morris also says the Greek tense of "caught" suggests she was "taken with her shame upon her." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-8/
- Steven Cole (bible.org): the scribes and Pharisees probably set a trap, using the woman to catch Jesus in a dilemma. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-45-caught-act-john-753-811

**v. 5:**
- Guzik: the trap had two sides. Letting her go would look like breaking Moses' law. Ordering her death would look harsh and break Roman law, since Rome had taken away the Jews' right to carry out executions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-8/
- Augustine: Jesus was known as gentle, so they attacked Him on righteousness instead. If He approved the stoning, He would lose His gentleness; if He let her go, He would seem to abandon justice. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701033.htm

**v. 6:**
- Guzik lists many guesses about what Jesus wrote: doodling, stalling, the law against her, Exodus 23:1, the accusers' names or sins. He sees the stooping as humility and as sharing the woman's humiliation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-8/
- Ellicott (biblehub): the likeliest meaning is that Jesus was refusing the role of judge, and writing on the ground was a known way of showing you were ignoring what was said. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/8-6.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: scholars have not been able to pin down the exact charge they hoped to bring against Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/8-6.htm
- Augustine: God's law was written by His finger on stone because hearts were hard. Christ now writes on the ground because He is looking for fruit. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701033.htm

**v. 7:**
- Guzik: under Jewish law the witnesses threw the first stones. Jesus didn't cancel the sentence. Instead He turned judgment on the accusers and demanded that justice be done fairly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-8/
- Augustine: Jesus' answer sent them back to examine themselves. Let the sinner be punished, but not by sinners. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701033.htm

**v. 8:**
- Ellicott: stooping again repeats His refusal to act as judge, while the law written on their hearts convicts them. One ancient manuscript adds that He wrote "the sin of each one of them." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill: He looked down to let the accusers slip away quietly. Expositor's Greek Testament: the gesture meant that, for Him, the matter was closed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/8-8.htm

**v. 9:**
- Ellicott: the phrase "convicted by their own conscience" (in some versions) was probably added by a copyist to explain the meaning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/8-9.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: conscience showed them that the spirit of the law is greater than its letter. Gill and others suggest the oldest left first because they had more sins to remember, or because they understood fastest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/8-9.htm
- Guzik: it speaks well of them that their consciences could still be stirred. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-8/
- Augustine: once they left, only two remained: the wretched woman and Mercy. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701033.htm

**v. 10:**
- Precept Austin: unlike the Pharisees, Jesus cared for her real needs and showed grace instead of condemnation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-8-commentary
- Augustine: having heard "without sin," she expected to be punished by the one person who was sinless. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701033.htm

**v. 11:**
- Ellicott: she makes no plea and no defence. "Lord" may be polite or reverent. Unlike other healing or forgiveness scenes, there is no spoken word of forgiveness here, yet the command to go sets her sin under judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm
- Augustine (Catholic): Jesus condemned the sin, not the person. If He favoured sin, He would have said "go, live as you will." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701033.htm
- GotQuestions: "sin no more" doesn't mean sinless perfection. It warns against going back to a sinful way of life, and the words both extended mercy and demanded holiness. https://www.gotquestions.org/go-and-sin-no-more.html
- GotQuestions: only God can forgive sin, so this act supports Jesus' identity as God. https://www.gotquestions.org/neither-do-I-condemn-you.html
- Bible Hub study notes: His forgiveness is not a license to keep sinning but a call to a new life. https://biblehub.com/john/8-11.htm

---

## Verses 12–30

**v. 12:**
- Ellicott: whoever follows Christ doesn't just have a light to walk by. Through sharing His life, they hold that light within. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Jesus outshines the temple lamps and the pillar of cloud because He holds and gives life. Gill: Jesus sets Himself against Moses and the rabbis, whom the Jews called "the light of the world." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/8-12.htm
- MacArthur (via Precept Austin): this claim follows on from 7:37–52 and alludes to the lamp-lighting ceremony at the Feast of Tabernacles. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-8-commentary

**v. 14:**
- Ellicott: "I" is emphatic. Jesus claims the normal rule of evidence doesn't really apply to Him. He also meets their own test from 7:27 that no one would know where the Messiah comes from. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm

**v. 16:**
- Ellicott: judging wasn't the aim of His coming, but it follows when the Light appears (3:19). When He does judge, His judgment matches the Father's truth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm

**v. 17:**
- Ellicott: this doesn't set Jesus against the law of Moses. The law asks for two men as witnesses; He has two Persons, both divine. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm

**v. 18:**
- Ellicott: the Greek has no word for "one." It reads more like "I am He who bears witness." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm

**v. 19:**
- Ellicott: a scornful question ("produce your second witness"). Jesus traces their ignorance of the Father to their rejection of Him, the only way God can be known. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm

**v. 20:**
- Ellicott: the "treasury" refers to the trumpet-shaped offering chests in the Court of the Women. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm

**v. 21:**
- Ellicott: the Greek is singular, "in your sin," meaning a state of sin. Verse 24 uses the plural for actual wrongdoing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm
- Cole (bible.org): Jesus warns that even if they look for Him later, they will still die in their sin and face judgment. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-47-terrible-words-loving-savior-john-821-29

**v. 22:**
- Ellicott: they sense a deeper meaning but can't see how it will happen. Any hint about suicide comes only from them; Jesus gives it no support. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm

**v. 23:**
- Ellicott: Jesus is from heaven and divine. In Him alone the divine and the human meet, and in Him alone deliverance from sin is found. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm

**v. 24:** (the key verse for "I am")
- Ligonier (Reformed): "I am he" translates the Greek *egō eimi*, with no "he" in the original. The phrase is used in the Greek Old Testament for God's own self-naming (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 40–55), so Jesus is saying we must believe He is God. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/how-not-die-sin
- Cole (bible.org): likewise, Jesus was probably saying "unless you believe that I am the Lord God." https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-47-terrible-words-loving-savior-john-821-29
- Ellicott (biblehub): "He" isn't in the Greek, but the listeners had been talking about the Messiah, which points toward a messianic meaning. Gill reads it fully: the eternal "I am," the true God and Messiah. Expositor's Greek Testament says Westcott's fuller meaning hardly fits the context and notes Meyer's reading, "that I am the Messiah." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/8-24.htm
- Translations differ: NASB, NAB (Catholic) and ISV have "I am" or "I AM," while most others have "I am he." https://biblehub.com/john/8-24.htm. Wesley's 1755 New Testament reads "that I am." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/john/8-24.html

**v. 25:**
- Ellicott: they ask "Who are you?" in the same scornful tone as verse 22. (The page cuts off here.) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/8.htm

**v. 28:**
- Gill: "lifted up" means the cross, like the bronze serpent on the pole (Numbers 21). What was meant to shame Him becomes His exaltation. Some will come to know Him to their shame, others to their salvation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/8-28.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the title "Son of Man" points to His real humanity, a man among men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/8-28.htm
- Cole: Jesus repeatedly stresses (vv. 16, 18, 26, 29) that the Father sent Him. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-47-terrible-words-loving-savior-john-821-29

**Verses with nothing found:** 13, 15, 26–27, 29 and 30. None of the pages I read discussed these on their own, apart from the brief mentions above.
